blocks.text: Amides contain the functional group –CO–NH₂. Since they are prepared from carboxylic acids that is why amides are still sometimes called as “acid amides”.
Amides can be prepared by the following methods.
1. By the reaction of acyl chlorides with ammonia

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-Cl + NH3 gives CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + HCl. Below: benzoyl chloride (ring-C(=O)-Cl) + NH3 gives benzamide (ring-C(=O)-NH2) + HCl.
blocks.caption: Amides from acyl chlorides and ammonia (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 127).

blocks.text: 2. By the reaction of acyl chlorides with primary amines

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-Cl (ethanoyl chloride) + CH3-CH2-NH2 gives CH3-C(=O)-NH-CH2-CH3 (N-ethyl ethanamide) + HCl. Below: CH3-C(=O)-Cl + phenyl amine gives CH3-C(=O)-NH-ring (N-phenyl ethanamide) + HCl.
blocks.caption: Amides from acyl chlorides and primary amines (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 127).

blocks.text: In the above two methods, all the reactions take place at room temperature, releasing white fumes of hydrogen chloride (HCl). The HCl produced reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt.

blocks.alt: R-NH2 + HCl gives R-NH3(+) Cl(-). Below: NH3 + HCl gives NH4(+) Cl(-).
blocks.caption: Salt formation by an amine and by ammonia with HCl (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.text: Therefore, an excess of ammonia or amine is used to ensure complete reaction.

All amides except methanamide, which is a liquid, are solid with sharp melting point. They have quite high boiling points which is a consequence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. However, in case of N-substituted amides, the melting and boiling points decrease as the sites for hydrogen bonding diminish with increasing number of alkyl substituents.

Amides are less basic than aliphatic amines. Unlike amines, amides form neutral solutions in water. They exhibit resonance where the lone pair on nitrogen participates in delocalization with oxygen of carbonyl group. This reduces the availability of electrons on nitrogen, thereby decreasing the basicity.

blocks.alt: R-C(=O)-NH2 with a lone pair on N and two curly arrows (the C=O electrons move onto O; the N lone pair moves into the C-N bond), a double-headed resonance arrow, and R-C(-O-)=NH2+.
blocks.caption: Resonance in an amide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.text: The introduction of double bond character between carbon and nitrogen reduces the C—N bond length less than the usual C—N single bond length.

blocks.alt: R-C(=O)-NH2 with an arrow to its C-N bond labelled (132 pm), and R-CH2-NH2 with an arrow to its C-N bond labelled (147 pm).
blocks.caption: C-N bond lengths in an amide and in an amine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.text: Amides are the least reactive of all acid derivatives, because lone pair of nitrogen is delocalized over the oxygen of carbonyl group, thus decreasing the electrophilic power (+δ charge) of the carbonyl carbon.
Reactions of amides are generally slow and require prolonged heating or catalysts (acid or base) for them to take place. Some of them are given as under:
Unsubstituted amides yield carboxylic acids ammonium salt.

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + H2O + HCl gives CH3-C(=O)-OH + NH4Cl.
blocks.caption: Acid hydrolysis of ethanamide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.text: In the base-catalyzed reaction, the products are the salts of carboxylic acids and ammonia. The free carboxylic acid is obtained when this salt is treated with dilute hydrochloric acid.

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + NaOH gives CH3-C(=O)-O-Na+ + NH3. Below: CH3-C(=O)-O-Na+ + HCl gives CH3-C(=O)-OH + NaCl.
blocks.caption: Base hydrolysis of ethanamide and acidification of the salt (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 129).

blocks.text: Amides are reduced to primary amines with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate (III) in dry ethoxyethane (ether).

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + 4[H], with LiAlH4 over and Dry ether under the arrow, gives CH3-CH2-NH2 + H2O. Below: benzamide (benzene ring-C(=O)-NH2) + 4[H] (LiAlH4, dry ether) gives ring-CH2-NH2 + H2O.
blocks.caption: Reduction of ethanamide and benzamide with LiAlH4 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 129).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed benzamide reduction draws both rings with only two C=C bonds; they are benzene rings (LiAlH₄ reduces only the C=O), as drawn above.
